content: Structured interviews were conducted with healthcare workers providing infant testing services, as well as semi-structured interviews with national and regional laboratory managers or early infant diagnosis program managers, both before and after the implementation of point-of-care (POC) infant testing in countries such as Swaziland, Kenya, Lesotho, Mozambique, Rwanda, and Zimbabwe. Healthcare workers reported that POC infant testing was user-friendly, with 74% describing it as very simple to perform. They expressed high satisfaction with the rapid turnaround time of results and the ability to initiate treatment for HIV-positive infants sooner, with 93% endorsing this benefit. All healthcare workers recommended scaling up POC infant testing in their respective countries, and 87% expressed a desire to have a POC testing device in their healthcare facilities. Laboratory managers also supported the expansion of POC testing but emphasized the importance of reliable infrastructure to support these platforms. An online survey was conducted among 51 healthcare workers and 53 program managers to assess the acceptability and feasibility of implementing POC infant testing. Among the healthcare workers surveyed, 88% felt comfortable performing the test, delivering results, counseling, and initiating treatment on the same day. Most healthcare workers (77%) believed POC testing would be acceptable, and 65% preferred it if available. Additionally, 88% thought mothers would accept same-day infant testing and, in some cases, positive diagnoses. However, 45% of healthcare workers anticipated an increased workload in clinics due to POC testing, though they believed sufficient human resources were available to implement it. Among the program managers surveyed, 72% reported that their countries already had policies for POC infant testing, but 85% noted that most infant tests were still conducted using standard laboratory-based methods. A majority (55%) considered POC infant testing both preferable and feasible. More than half (55%) did not believe that implementing POC testing would increase the workload in laboratories or clinics. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of POC technologies. The overall performance of these technologies demonstrated greater than 98% sensitivity and 99% specificity. Several POC technologies are currently available on the market, with two already prequalified by the World Health Organization (WHO). Devices such as the Abbott m-PIMA™ and Cepheid GeneXpert® are widely used for tuberculosis (TB) testing and early infant diagnosis. These devices utilize whole blood and do not require additional equipment or specialized expertise. The Abbott m-PIMA™ can process 6–8 tests per day, while the GeneXpert® can perform 6–8 tests per module per day. Across 140 high-burden developing countries, more than 11,600 GeneXpert® devices, comprising 52,000 modules, have been delivered, with current usage at two tests per module per day. This leaves capacity for expanding TB testing and considering HIV infant testing. Infant diagnosis should remain a priority when technologies are shared across programs. In most high HIV-burden countries, a small proportion of healthcare facilities serve the majority of HIV-exposed infants. For example, in Malawi, Mozambique, Uganda, and Zambia, 80% of HIV-exposed infants attended 32%, 33%, 12%, and 10% of healthcare facilities, respectively. This suggests that modest procurement and targeted placement of POC technologies could significantly impact HIV-exposed infants. Furthermore, 10% of healthcare facilities in these countries serve 49%, 46%, 75%, and 80% of HIV-exposed infants, respectively. Ethical and equity considerations were developed to guide discussions on POC testing implementation. These considerations emphasized the fair distribution of benefits and burdens at the population level (social justice), treating individuals as equally important (equity), and ensuring that infants are not disadvantaged compared to others in their communities. If the introduction of POC testing does not harm the broader community by diverting resources, there is little justification against its implementation. The WHO Guideline Development Group strongly recommended POC nucleic acid testing (NAT) for diagnosing HIV in infants and children under 18 months of age. This recommendation was based on the overwhelming benefits of the intervention, including faster testing and result delivery, improved retention in the testing-to-treatment cascade, fewer healthcare visits for caregivers, increased equity with adult HIV testing, faster access to antiretroviral therapy (ART), and improved service quality. No significant harms were identified, though higher costs, the need for extensive network support, and greater technical support and maintenance requirements were noted. Implementation considerations highlighted the need for ongoing expansion of high-quality diagnostic testing across HIV and other molecular testing needs, ideally integrating laboratory-based and POC technologies into a unified diagnostic network. If POC testing is not feasible, rapid laboratory-based testing should be ensured. Optimal placement of POC technologies should consider the overall health system context, including other disease programs and needs, to maximize efficiency and improve diagnostic services for HIV and other diseases. Adequate human resources, training, service and maintenance, and quality assurance must be carefully addressed. Clear communication and collaboration with community groups are essential to support demand generation, scale-up, trust, and utilization. Research gaps remain, particularly in quality assurance approaches for sustainable POC testing delivery. Investigating dual-claim POC tests for infants, children, and adults, which could streamline supply chains and diagnostic systems, is recommended. Additionally, device-free tests resembling traditional rapid diagnostic tests are under development, which could further decentralize testing and eliminate the need for capital investment in low-volume healthcare facilities. Diagnostic accuracy and clinical impact studies for these tests would be beneficial. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HIV serology can assess HIV exposure in infants younger than four months. However, these tests cannot distinguish between maternal HIV antibodies and those produced by the child. A positive HIV antibody test in infants under 18 months confirms exposure but not infection. In contrast, HIV antibodies in children older than 18 months reliably indicate infection, as maternal antibodies are no longer detectable. Children who start ART early (3–6 months of age) may not develop an antibody response and could falsely test HIV-negative using serological assays. Therefore, antibody testing should not be used to confirm or rule out infection in children already receiving ART. RDTs with performance comparable to traditional laboratory-based serological assays are commercially available and recommended by WHO for use in resource-limited settings. These tests can be performed in clinics or community settings with minimal infrastructure. However, RDTs may not reliably capture HIV-exposed infants older than four months. Testing mothers is the most reliable method to ascertain exposure and should be prioritized. When maternal testing is not possible, RDTs can reliably assess exposure in infants younger than four months. For infants and children aged 4–18 months, a positive RDT result establishes exposure, but a negative result does not rule out potential exposure. Infants with a positive RDT result require NAT to confirm infection. Implementation of RDTs for infants and children supports increased access to HIV testing in rural and remote areas. However, uptake of facility-based testing and counseling for children has been poor due to legal age of consent issues, provider discomfort with disclosure, and perceived lack of importance in testing asymptomatic children. Addressing these barriers and ensuring linkage to care for exposed or infected children is critical.
